etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English bras, bres, from Old English bræs (“brass, bronze”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps representing a backformation from Proto-Germanic *brasnaz (“brazen”), from or related to *brasō (“fire, pyre”). Compare Old Norse and Icelandic bras (“solder”), Icelandic brasa (“to harden in the fire”), Swedish brasa (“a small controlled fire”), Danish brase (“to fry”); French braser ("to solder"; > English braise) from the same Germanic root. Compare also Middle Dutch braspenninc ("a silver coin", literally, "silver-penny"; > Dutch braspenning), Old Frisian bress (“copper”), Middle Low German bras (“metal, ore”).

In the military sense an ellipsis of the brass hats.

definitions.definition: A memorial or sepulchral tablet usually made of brass or latten.
Fittings, utensils, or other items made of brass.
(countable, uncountable) A metallic alloy of copper and zinc used in many industrial and plumbing applications.
(music) A class of wind instruments, usually made of metal (such as brass), that use vibrations of the player's lips to produce sound; the section of an orchestra that features such instruments
Spent shell casings (usually made of brass); the part of the cartridge left over after bullets have been fired.
(military, business or other organizations, uncountable, used as a singular or plural noun, metonymically) High-ranking officers.

quote.citation: 2004 November 9, Bungie, Halo 2, spoken by Avery Johnson (David Scully), Microsoft Game Studios, Xbox, level/area: The Armory:
quote.text: I don't want to keep the brass waiting, Chief.

definitions.definition: (uncountable, informal) A brave or foolhardy attitude; impudence.
Made of brass, of or pertaining to brass.

quote.text: At the Council board, I hope to charge him with that he cannot answer, and yet I know his face is brass enough.

quote.citation: 1872, Elsie Leigh Whittlesey, Helen Ethinger: or, Not Exactly Right, page 154:
quote.text: [...] he continued in the same insulting strain. "If you were not quite brass, you would know it is not proper to be making promises you dare not tell of."
It was a show of very large and very brass cojones, [...]

quote.text: Maybe (probably so), but it's rare someone is brass enough to post a msg for all to see asking for a software key, that the vast majority have paid for in support of the development effort.

definitions.definition: (slang) Bad, annoying; as wordplay applied especially to brass instruments.

quote.citation: 1888, Mr. & Mrs. Bancroft on and off the stage: written by themselves, volume 1, page 90:
quote.text: Grindoff, the miller, 'and the leader of a very brass band of most unpopular performers, with a thorough base accompaniment of at least fifty vices,' was played by Miss Saunders.

quote.citation: 1900 November 3, “The Training of Seamen”, in The Saturday Review, volume 90, number 2349, page 556:
quote.text: I must confess that to me there is something almost pathetic in the sight of a body of bluejackets improving their muscles on the quarter deck by bar-bell exercise, accompanied by a brass — a very brass — band, [...]

quote.citation: 1908, The Smith Family, published in Punch, March 4 1908, bound in Punch vol. CXXXIV, page 168:
quote.text: Mr. REGINALD SMITH, KC, the publisher, followed, but he had hardly begun his very interesting remarks when a procession headed by a very brass band entered Smithfield from the west, and approached the platform.

quote.citation: 1937, Blair Niles, A journey in time: Peruvian pageant, page 166:
quote.text: There are soldiers, policemen, priests and friars, as well as a motley mass of women, children, babies and dogs, and upon special occasions a very brass band.

The padre in my neighborhood — Santa Ana — was having some kind of a fiesta, and had hired a very brass band. This band kept up its martial airs for hours and hours after I got home, with grand finales — or what each time I hoped would be the grand finale, every five minutes.

quote.citation: 1939, The New York times film reviews, volume 3:
quote.text: As Honest Plush Brannon then, Mr. Beery is one of San Francisco's fancier con men and hence more brass than plush

etymologies.etymologyHTML: By ellipsis from brass nail, in turn from "nail[ing]" (fig.) and "brass blonde" (see "brazen"); and also shortened from Cockney Rhyming slang brass flute for "prostitute".

quote.citation: 1996, Will Self, The Sweet Smell of Psychosis, Bloomsbury, published 2011, page 2:
quote.text: Richard didn't want the man on the corner to go up and fuck one of the brasses.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Portuguese braça and Spanish braza, from Old Galician-Portuguese and Old Spanish braça, from Latin brachia, variant of bracchium (“arm, cubit”), from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn, “upper arm”).

definitions.definition: (historical, obsolete) Synonym of brace, a traditional unit of measure equivalent to a fathom (6 feet) or about 1.6 m, especially as the Spanish braza and Portuguese braça, also French brasse.
